Just now

--

A technical explainer on authorship verification, the data that makes it feasible at scale, and what a privacy-conscious reader can do about it.
Written by Jesse C — Founder @ Veilfire. Visit veilfire.io to see Safe, Secure, Ethical Artificial Intelligence.

The signal that rides inside the content
Almost every tracking technology in commercial use shares a hidden weakness: it attaches to something outside the message. A cookie lives in browser storage. A tracking pixel fires from a third-party domain and reports back. A device fingerprint is assembled from your screen resolution, fonts, GPU, and time zone. Each of these is a tag placed onto you or your hardware, and because it is placed on rather than woven in, it can, at least in principle, be removed. Clear the cookie, block the pixel, harden the browser, switch devices, and the tag is gone or degraded.
Linguistic stylometry is different in kind. The identifying signal is not attached to your content; it is your content. The rate at which you reach for “however” rather than “but,” your comma habits, your sentence rhythm, the particular function words you overuse without noticing: these travel inside every paragraph you write, on every platform, under every pseudonym, from every device. There is nothing to clear, because the thing doing the identifying is the writing itself.
This is not a new academic curiosity. As early as 2012, researchers showed that writing style alone could pick an anonymous author out of a pool of 100,000 candidates with meaningful accuracy [1], and the field has since moved from hand-counted function words to neural models that map an author’s style into a numerical vector and compare millions of people at once [2], [3]. What is new, and what motivates this article, is the arrival of a data source well suited to feeding these methods: the large language model chat interface, into which hundreds of millions of people now type first-person prose, labelled by account, day after day, in close to the exact form a stylometric system wants.
This piece is organized around four claims, presented in order of increasing strength. The first is that the capability to fingerprint and link authors by writing style is real and demonstrated on real data. The second is that commercial AI providers now hold and retain the kind of corpus that would make such fingerprinting unusually effective. The third is that the incentives and existing product features make some form of persistent, per-user modeling plausible rather than far-fetched. The fourth, which keeps the other three in proportion, is that there is at present no public evidence that any major provider actually builds cross-internet stylometric trackers to de-anonymize its users. The distance between what is possible and what is known to be happening does a great deal of work in what follows, and I have tried to keep it visible. The aim is to understand a capability well enough to decide what, if anything, to do about it.
How authorship verification works
It is worth being precise about the task. Authorship attribution asks: given this text and a fixed list of candidates, which one wrote it? Authorship verification asks a subtler question: given a body of writing known to come from person X, and a new sample of unknown origin, did X write the new sample, even though the true author might be someone not on any list [4]? Verification is the relevant framing for tracking, because a tracker rarely has a tidy suspect list. It has a profile of a target, built from known writing, and a stream of anonymous content to test against that profile.
The central and somewhat surprising finding of the field is that the most discriminating features are the least meaningful ones. Topic words tell you what a text is about; function words, punctuation, and character sequences tell you who wrote it, because they are produced unconsciously and stay roughly constant regardless of subject [4], [5]. A classical verifier leans on those high-frequency features and measures distance. A modern one does something more powerful.
Since around 2021 the strongest results have come from contrastive author embeddings. Models such as LUAR are trained on very large datasets, in LUAR’s case roughly a million Reddit authors, to project any writing sample into a fixed-length style vector, learning to place two samples by the same person close together and samples by different people far apart [2]. Verification then reduces to measuring the cosine similarity between two vectors against a calibrated threshold. A later system, STAR, trained on 4.5 million texts from 70,000 authors, can distinguish an author from a pool of more than 1,600 candidates at over 80 percent accuracy using only eight short documents [3]. These systems scale to populations that classical methods never could, and, importantly for the tracking scenario, they are built to work on short, social-media-length text rather than on novels.
Short text is still the hard case. Classical methods need a large sample to stabilize their statistics; the reliable floor for distance-based verification sits somewhere around 2,500 to 5,000 words per sample, and results below a few thousand words degrade sharply [6]. A single chat prompt of 75 to 150 words is far below that line. The technique that rescues short-text verification is aggregation: pooling many short samples from the same identity into one richer profile. Neural encoders build this in, combining up to sixteen short documents before comparison [2]. This is why a multi-turn conversation, say eight to sixteen turns totaling a few hundred words, is a far stronger signal than any single prompt. The more you write under one identity, the sharper the fingerprint becomes.
Why this is a tracking signal unlike the others
Set stylometry beside the tools the advertising industry actually uses and its distinguishing properties come into focus. The breakdown below compares five identification technologies across the dimensions that matter for persistent tracking.
1. Third-party cookies
Attaches to: browser storage
Survives cookie clearing: no
Survives VPN or incognito: VPN yes, incognito no
Survives a new device: no
Links pseudonymous accounts: rarely
Needs code on the page: no, the server sets it
You can remove it: yes, clear cookies
2. Tracking pixels (for example the Meta Pixel)
Attaches to: browser plus logged-in identity graph
Survives cookie clearing: largely no
Survives VPN or incognito: VPN yes
Survives a new device: no
Links pseudonymous accounts: yes, through the logged-in identity
Needs code on the page: yes, the site must embed it
You can remove it: partly, by clearing cookies and blocking trackers
3. Browser and device fingerprinting
Attaches to: device plus browser configuration
Survives cookie clearing: yes
Survives VPN or incognito: yes
Survives a new device: no
Links pseudonymous accounts: within one device, not across devices
Needs code on the page: yes, JavaScript
You can remove it: hard, requires a hardened browser
4. Behavioral biometrics (keystroke and mouse dynamics)
Attaches to: input behavior
Survives cookie clearing: yes
Survives VPN or incognito: yes
Survives a new device: partly
Links pseudonymous accounts: potentially, on instrumented sites
Needs code on the page: yes, it must capture input events
You can remove it: hard
5. Stylometric fingerprinting
Attaches to: the content itself, which is to say the person
Survives cookie clearing: yes
Survives VPN or incognito: yes
Survives a new device: yes
Links pseudonymous accounts: yes
Needs code on the page: no, only the text is needed
You can remove it: only by changing how you write
The contrast is quite clear. Browser fingerprinting is genuinely persistent: it survives cookie deletion, a VPN, and incognito mode, because it reads characteristics the browser reports regardless of browsing mode [7], [8]. But it is tied to a specific device and browser build, so a new laptop or a major software change can break the link. Behavioral biometrics such as keystroke dynamics are similarly persistent but require the tracker to run code that captures your typing rhythm as you type; with no capture, there is no signal.
Stylometry is the only technology in the table that is at once persistent across cookie-clearing and VPNs, portable across devices, able to link distinct pseudonymous accounts, and free of any need for instrumentation. It requires nothing but the words, which the target hands over voluntarily and publicly every time they post. The only way a user removes the identifier is to change how they write, and, as the section on countermeasures shows, that is harder than it sounds.
The capability is demonstrated, not hypothetical
The first of the four claims is the easiest to establish, because the demonstrations already exist on real data.
The foundational result is Narayanan and colleagues’ 2012 study, which tested stylometric identification at what the authors called internet scale. Drawing on a corpus of tens of thousands of blogs, they showed that in over 20 percent of cases their classifier could correctly identify an anonymous author out of 100,000 candidates on the first guess, with the true author appearing among the top twenty guesses about 35 percent of the time. More telling for a tracker’s purposes, when the system was allowed to decline uncertain cases and answer only when confident, the precision of its top guess rose from roughly 20 percent to over 80 percent [1]. A tracker does not need to identify everyone; it needs to identify someone, confidently, some of the time, and confidence-thresholded stylometry does exactly that. The subjects in that study took no steps to disguise their writing [1].
The cross-account linking case is even more relevant, and it comes from security research rather than theory. The Doppelgänger Finder system was built to find users operating multiple accounts across underground cybercrime forums. In its one-to-many mode, matching an unknown author against a set of suspects, it reached 77 to 84 percent accuracy on private messages. In its unsupervised mode, taking an entire forum and surfacing likely same-person account pairs, it achieved 94 percent recall at 90 percent precision on blogs, and roughly 85 percent precision on real underground-forum users, uncovering previously undetected duplicate accounts on the live Carders forum [9]. The important detail is that this was unsupervised and used simple character-level features: no labels, no suspect list, only a pile of anonymous writing and the question of which pieces share an author. That is the tracking primitive in its purest form.
Short, conversational text is not a refuge either. Researchers have demonstrated stylometric linkability of individual tweets [10], and cross-domain work has linked the same authors across blogs, Twitter, and Reddit, though with a caveat that recurs below: accuracy falls when moving between platforms, from 83.5 percent within a single domain to 34.3 percent across domains, with domain-adaptation techniques recovering it to around 70 percent [11]. Part of that drop reflects a well-studied difficulty in separating style from topic, since a model can end up keying on what a person tends to write about rather than how they write [12]. The signal survives the jump between platforms; it simply gets noisier.
The commercial substrate: who now holds the corpus
Here the argument turns to its more uncomfortable middle claim. Stylometric identification has always had one practical bottleneck: you need a substantial, clean, identity-labelled corpus of the target’s writing to build the profile in the first place. Historically that corpus was scattered and hard to assemble. The large language model chat interface has changed this for whoever holds the logs.
Consider what a conversational AI product collects that a pixel network does not. It receives long-form, first-person prose rather than click
